records.title: Madam Koi Koi: The High-Heeled Ghost of Boarding Schools
records.summary: The undisputed terror of Nigerian secondary boarding school dormitories since the late 1970s, Madam Koi Koi is the vengeful spirit of an exceptionally glamorous, cruel schoolteacher notorious for wearing striking red high-heeled shoes. Fired after slapping a student so hard that the child suffered permanent injury, she was killed in an accident while traveling home, vowing vengeance on all students. Nocturnal boarding school students report waking in absolute darkness to the distinct, echoing rhythm of high heels clicking down the hallway tiles: 'Koi... koi... koi...' Anyone who peeks through the dormitory window or fails to close their eyes is slapped blind or snatched away into the night.
records.region_or_community: Secondary boarding schools nationwide across Nigeria
community_attributions: Nigerian boarding school student oral network
geographic_associations: Federal Government Colleges and boarding schools across Nigeria

records.title: Bush Baby: The Crying Infant Demon with the Golden Mat
records.summary: A dreaded supernatural entity of Nigerian boarding school compounds and overgrown school orchards, Bush Baby manifests as a small, hideous demon resembling an infant or diminutive primate carrying a small woven straw mat (eni) and a magical lantern. Crouching beneath mango and cashew trees on dark nights, it mimics the agonizing, pitiful cries of an abandoned newborn baby to lure sympathetic students outside into the bush. Urban legend holds that if someone manages to steal the Bush Baby's woven mat, the demon will follow them for seven days pleading for its return, making the thief fabulously wealthy if they endure the terrifying supernatural torment.
records.region_or_community: Boarding school bush peripheries throughout Nigeria
geographic_associations: School compounds across Southwestern and Southeastern Nigeria

records.title: Lady of the Long Legs: The Highway Phantom of Lagos
records.summary: A widely circulated motorist urban legend in Lagos centers on the desolate, poorly lit stretches of the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway and the Ikorodu highway after midnight. Drivers traveling late report glancing out their windshield to see an impossibly tall, slender woman whose legs extend over twenty feet into the air, straddling the entire multilane highway like a living bridge. Vehicles that pass beneath her legs experience sudden total engine failure, headlights blowing out, and violent steering shudder, warning drivers against traveling the intercity motorways during ungodly midnight hours.
alternate_names: The Giant Woman of the Expressway
records.region_or_community: Lagos State and Ogun State highway corridors

records.title: The Phantom Okada Rider of Third Mainland Bridge
records.summary: Stretching nearly twelve kilometers across the Lagos Lagoon, the Third Mainland Bridge is one of Africa's longest bridges and the focus of numerous nocturnal urban legends. Late-night motorists report encountering a lone commercial motorcyclist (okada rider) carrying a silent, passenger clad in black who speeds past them at breakneck velocity. As overtaking drivers watch in horror, the motorcycle abruptly swerves and plunges straight over the side railings into the black lagoon waters below. Motorists who stop discover the barrier completely intact, with no splash or ripples in the dark water below.
alternate_names: The Lagoon Jumper of Third Mainland Bridge

records.title: The Ghost Train of the Jebba River Bridge
records.summary: Crossing the mighty Niger River in Kwara State, the historic Jebba railway bridge, completed in 1916 by British colonial authorities, is adjacent to the monument of 19th-century explorer Mungo Park. Railway maintenance workers and local fishermen recount urban legends of a phantom colonial steam train that roars across the iron truss bridge during midnight rainstorms, blaring a piercing steam whistle with furnace sparks flying from the smokestack. The phantom train vanishes into the mist upon reaching the middle span, commemorating fatal derailments during early bridge construction.
records.region_or_community: Jebba, Kwara and Niger State border

records.title: The Cursed Currency of the Okija Shrine
records.summary: Located in Ihiala, Anambra State, the Ogwugwu Akpu Okija shrine became world-famous in August 2004 when Nigerian police raided the dense forest sanctuary, uncovering dozens of decomposing corpses deposited by devotees who swore oaths before the shrine's deities and perished after lying. In southeastern Nigerian urban folklore, currency obtained through corrupt oaths or blood money associated with Okija is said to be spiritually cursed: paper banknotes spontaneously turn into dried leaves or slithering snakes inside wallets, bringing sudden ruin, madness, and unexplainable sickness upon greed-driven exploiters.
records.historical_period: 2004 Police Raid to Living Contemporary Legend

records.title: Mami Wata Sighting at Bar Beach Lagos
records.summary: A pan-African water deity deeply anchored in modern Nigerian coastal urban lore, Mami Wata is venerated as an exquisite, fair-skinned water spirit with long cascading dark hair, adorned with heavy gold jewelry and draped with a large serpent around her shoulders. In Lagos during the 1980s and 1990s along the storm-tossed sands of Bar Beach (now Eko Atlantic), beachgoers and fishermen repeatedly reported seeing her emerge from the crashing Atlantic foam at midnight, brushing her hair with a golden comb. Legend warns that she offers vast material wealth to devotees in exchange for absolute fidelity, taking the lives of those who break their spiritual vows.
alternate_names: The Water Mermaid of Victoria Island
geographic_associations: Bar Beach (Eko Atlantic), Victoria Island, Lagos

records.title: The Midnight Knock of the Evil Spirit in Enugu
records.summary: During the mid-1990s in the coal city of Enugu in southeastern Nigeria, an acute urban panic swept residential neighborhoods regarding a malevolent nocturnal entity known as 'The Midnight Knocker.' According to terrified residents, three loud, heavy knocks would sound on residential wooden doors at 2:00 AM, accompanied by a polite voice calling the homeowner by their full real name. Urban folklore warned that anyone who opened the door or answered the greeting would collapse instantly and perish by sunrise, causing entire neighborhoods to stay awake praying with church bells ringing until dawn.
alternate_names: The Nocturnal Visitor of Coal City
records.region_or_community: Enugu metropolis, Enugu State, Southeastern Nigeria

records.title: The Vanishing Cloth Merchant of Onitsha Main Market
records.summary: Sprawling along the eastern bank of the River Niger, the Onitsha Main Market is renowned as the largest commercial market in West Africa. A famous commercial urban legend involves rich foreign cloth buyers who arrive at luxury lace and Dutch wax stalls in the bustling market. After selecting dozens of expensive textile bales and handing the shopkeeper thick bundles of crisp currency, the merchant walks toward the riverbank to arrange boat transit. When the stall owner later opens their cash drawer, the money has dissolved into river sand and dead leaves, with the mysterious buyer vanishing into the Niger River mist.

records.title: The Whispering Baobab of Ancient Kano City Walls
records.summary: Dating back to the 11th century, the Ancient Kano City Walls (Badalar Kano) were a fourteen-kilometer defensive mud rampart guarding the historic emirate. Near the historic Kofar Nassarawa gate stands a massive, ancient baobab tree (Kuka) that is the focus of Hausa spirit lore (Bori). Night pedestrians report hearing whispers and rustling voices emanating from the hollow trunk when there is no wind, attributed to ancestral spirits and djinn who gathered to advise the ancient Emirs of Kano during wartime. Local superstition strictly prohibits breaking branches from the sacred tree after sunset.
alternate_names: The Spirit Baobab of Kofar Nassarawa
